items.stem: State what is meant by the term "research question".
items.answer: A focused, open question that the historical investigation sets out to answer
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a focused, open question that the historical investigation sets out to answer. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why availability of sources should influence the choice of topic.
items.answer: Without accessible primary and secondary sources, the student cannot evaluate evidence or support an argument.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Without accessible primary and secondary sources, the student cannot evaluate evidence or support an argument. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why availability of sources should influence the choice of topic.
items.answer: Without accessible primary and secondary sources, the student cannot evaluate evidence or support an argument. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Without accessible primary and secondary sources, the student cannot evaluate evidence or support an argument. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from R. G. Collingwood, British philosopher and historian, The Idea of History, published 1946

Every step in the argument depends on asking a question. The historian does not wait for the evidence to speak; he puts the evidence to the question.

Explain the view of framing a focused historical research question that is presented in Source A.
items.answer: Historical knowledge is created by asking questions of evidence rather than waiting for it to reveal the past.
items.markingKey: Historical knowledge is created by asking questions of evidence rather than waiting for it to reveal the past. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]. Points must come from the source itself; own knowledge is not credited in this question.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from John Tosh, British historian, The Pursuit of History, 1984 (later editions to 2021)

Research begins with a problem, not a topic. A well-defined question guides the search for sources and prevents the historian from drowning in material.

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for an historian studying framing a focused historical research question.
items.answer: Value: A widely used guide to historical method by an experienced historian. Limitations: It is a general methodological text, not evidence from a particular research project.
items.markingKey: Value: A widely used guide to historical method by an experienced historian. Limitations: It is a general methodological text, not evidence from a particular research project. Award up to [3]: the response must refer to origin, purpose and content and link each to value or limitation for the stated enquiry; at least one value and one limitation are needed for full marks; a list of features without explaining their effect on value is capped at half marks.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from R. G. Collingwood, British philosopher and historian, The Idea of History, published 1946

Every step in the argument depends on asking a question. The historian does not wait for the evidence to speak; he puts the evidence to the question.

Source B: Paraphrased from John Tosh, British historian, The Pursuit of History, 1984 (later editions to 2021)

Research begins with a problem, not a topic. A well-defined question guides the search for sources and prevents the historian from drowning in material.

“The research question is the most important factor in the success of a historical investigation.” Using Sources A and B and your own knowledge, how far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: A strong question is necessary, but success also depends on analysis and evaluation of sources.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – supporting: focus and scope; determines source selection; enables argument. Challenging: quality of sources; analysis and evaluation; reflection on method. Judgement: A strong question is necessary, but success also depends on analysis and evaluation of sources. Candidates must use both sources and their own knowledge; Markbands – 6–8: focused response; effective use of the sources and accurate own knowledge, integrated (synthesised) to support a clear, balanced judgement; 4–5: some focus on the question; uses sources or own knowledge, with some analysis but little synthesis; 1–3: limited understanding; generalised comments, sources or own knowledge used descriptively; 0: does not reach the standard of the descriptors below.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "scope"?
options: The extent to which a source’s information can be trusted for a given purpose
The historian’s choice of which evidence to use, which shapes the argument
A focused, open question that the historical investigation sets out to answer
The limits of an investigation in time, place and subject, which keep it manageable
items.answer: The limits of an investigation in time, place and subject, which keep it manageable
items.markingKey: D. "scope" is the limits of an investigation in time, place and subject, which keep it manageable.

items.stem: Outline one way in which refining a broad topic on Kosovo shows the process of framing a research question.
items.answer: “Kosovo in the 1990s” was narrowed to “To what extent did the Dayton Agreement (1995) cause the shift from non-violent to armed resistance among Kosovo Albanians by 1998?” The refined question is focused in time, place and issue and invites a supported judgement.
items.markingKey: Context (“Kosovo in the 1990s” was narrowed to “To what extent did the Dayton Agreement (1995) cause the shift from non-violent to armed resistance among Kosovo Albanians by 1998?”) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The refined question is focused in time, place and issue and invites a supported judgement. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the process of framing a research question.

items.stem: In 1983 which German magazine published forged “Hitler Diaries”?
options: Bild
Stern
Die Zeit
Der Spiegel
items.answer: Stern
items.markingKey: B. Forensic tests showed post-war materials; the forger was Konrad Kujau.

items.stem: "A source is useless if it is biased." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Bias may make a source valuable as evidence of attitudes and perspectives.
items.markingKey: Bias may make a source valuable as evidence of attitudes and perspectives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why it is important to evaluate sources in relation to the research question.
items.answer: The same source can be very valuable for one question and limited for another; evaluation must explain how origin, purpose and content affect its value for the specific investigation. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The same source can be very valuable for one question and limited for another; evaluation must explain how origin, purpose and content affect its value for the specific investigation. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to the Hitler Diaries hoax of 1983, explain how it illustrates the importance of verifying authenticity.
items.answer: Stern paid millions of marks for 60 volumes; forensic tests found that the paper and glue contained post-war whiteners. It showed that even eminent historians and editors can be deceived without forensic and provenance checks.
items.markingKey: Context (Stern paid millions of marks for 60 volumes; forensic tests found that the paper and glue contained post-war whiteners.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It showed that even eminent historians and editors can be deceived without forensic and provenance checks. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of verifying authenticity.

items.stem:
Source B: Paraphrased from Hugh Trevor-Roper, British historian, article in The Times, 23 April 1983

I am satisfied that the documents are authentic; and that the standard accounts of Hitler’s behaviour will have to be revised.

Assess the usefulness of Source B to an historian investigating identifying and evaluating sources for a historical investigation, referring to who produced it, when, why and what it contains.
items.answer: Value: Written by an eminent historian of Hitler, it shows how the forgery initially convinced experts. Limitations: Trevor-Roper had little time to examine the diaries and did not read German handwriting well; he later withdrew his judgement.
items.markingKey: Value: Written by an eminent historian of Hitler, it shows how the forgery initially convinced experts. Limitations: Trevor-Roper had little time to examine the diaries and did not read German handwriting well; he later withdrew his judgement. Award up to [3]: the response must refer to origin, purpose and content and link each to value or limitation for the stated enquiry; at least one value and one limitation are needed for full marks; a list of features without explaining their effect on value is capped at half marks.

items.stem:
Source C: Paraphrased from Hugh Trevor-Roper, British historian, article in The Times, 23 April 1983

I am satisfied that the documents are authentic; and that the standard accounts of Hitler’s behaviour will have to be revised.

Summarise the argument conveyed by Source C in relation to identifying and evaluating sources for a historical investigation.
items.answer: The diaries are authentic and will change historians’ understanding of Hitler.
items.markingKey: The diaries are authentic and will change historians’ understanding of Hitler. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]. Points must come from the source itself; own knowledge is not credited in this question.

items.stem: Evaluate the value and limitations of oral history for a historical investigation on the Rwandan genocide.
items.answer: Oral history is invaluable for experience but must be corroborated and evaluated carefully.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: survivor and perpetrator testimony; memory and trauma; political pressures in Rwanda; corroboration. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Oral history is invaluable for experience but must be corroborated and evaluated carefully. Markbands – 13–15: clearly focused, well structured response; accurate and relevant knowledge used effectively; well-chosen examples; evaluation of different perspectives; all main points substantiated; reasoned, consistent conclusion; 10–12: clear awareness of the demands; clearly structured; accurate, relevant knowledge placed in context; analysis with most points substantiated; some awareness of different perspectives; 7–9: demands understood but not all implications considered; mostly accurate knowledge; some critical analysis, though partly narrative; 4–6: some indication of the demands; some knowledge but lacking accuracy or relevance; mostly narrative or descriptive, limited analysis; 1–3: little understanding of the demands of the question; poorly structured, little relevant knowledge, no analysis; 0: does not reach the standard of the descriptors below.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that primary sources are always more useful than secondary sources in a historical investigation.
items.answer: Both are essential; their usefulness depends on the research question and evaluation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: direct evidence of the past; enable original analysis; show contemporary perspectives. Arguments against: secondary sources provide context and interpretations; primary sources may be forged or biased; usefulness depends on the question. Supported judgement: Both are essential; their usefulness depends on the research question and evaluation. Markbands: Use the IB Paper 2/3 markbands, scaled to the marks: top band – clearly focused, well structured, accurate and relevant knowledge used to support critical analysis, different perspectives evaluated, reasoned conclusion; middle band – mostly accurate knowledge, some analysis but partly narrative; lower band – little understanding of the demands, mainly description.

items.stem: Explain why oral history interviews can be both valuable and limited.
items.answer: They provide personal experiences unavailable elsewhere but are affected by memory, hindsight, the interviewer’s questions and the interviewee’s purposes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They provide personal experiences unavailable elsewhere but are affected by memory, hindsight, the interviewer’s questions and the interviewee’s purposes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Websites should never be used in a historical investigation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Websites can be used if their origin is credible and they are evaluated critically, e.g. digitised archives or academic sites.
items.markingKey: Websites can be used if their origin is credible and they are evaluated critically, e.g. digitised archives or academic sites. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source C: Paraphrased from the report of the West German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv) on the “Hitler Diaries”, 6 May 1983

Tests showed that the paper contained a whitening agent not used in paper until the 1950s, and the bindings contained polyester threads. The diaries are a crude forgery.

An historian is researching identifying and evaluating sources for a historical investigation. Explain the value and limitations of Source C for this research, with reference to its origin, purpose and content.
items.answer: Value: An official scientific examination by the national archives, giving conclusive evidence about authenticity. Limitations: It addresses only authenticity and does not explain how the forgery was produced or why experts were deceived.
items.markingKey: Value: An official scientific examination by the national archives, giving conclusive evidence about authenticity. Limitations: It addresses only authenticity and does not explain how the forgery was produced or why experts were deceived. Award up to [4]: the response must refer to origin, purpose and content and link each to value or limitation for the stated enquiry; at least one value and one limitation are needed for full marks; a list of features without explaining their effect on value is capped at half marks.

items.stem: Who wrote “The Return of Martin Guerre” (1983), reflecting on the role of invention in historical reconstruction?
options: E. H. Carr
Natalie Zemon Davis
Richard Evans
Pierre Nora
items.answer: Natalie Zemon Davis
items.markingKey: B. Davis described her reconstruction as partly invention, held in check by the voices of the past.

items.stem: "The reflection should summarise the investigation’s findings." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Reflection should focus on the methods and challenges of history, linked to the investigation, not repeat the conclusion.
items.markingKey: Reflection should focus on the methods and challenges of history, linked to the investigation, not repeat the conclusion. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the investigation section and the reflection section.
items.answer: The investigation presents an argument answering the research question using evidence; the reflection considers what the process revealed about the methods and challenges of historians.
items.markingKey: The investigation presents an argument answering the research question using evidence; the reflection considers what the process revealed about the methods and challenges of historians. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source C: Paraphrased from Richard J. Evans, British historian, In Defence of History, 1997

History can be true, if not absolutely so. The past did happen, and historians can, with care and honesty, reach reliable, if provisional, conclusions about it.

Explain the view of organising an argument and reflecting on the methods of historians that is presented in Source C.
items.answer: Historians can reach reliable, though not absolute, truths about the past if they work carefully.
items.markingKey: Historians can reach reliable, though not absolute, truths about the past if they work carefully. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]. Points must come from the source itself; own knowledge is not credited in this question.

items.stem: With reference to Natalie Zemon Davis’s work on the sixteenth-century impostor Arnaud du Tilh, explain how it illustrates the challenges historians face with limited evidence.
items.answer: Davis combined court records with informed speculation to reconstruct the lives of peasants in a famous case of identity fraud. It shows how historians must use imagination carefully when evidence is incomplete, and be transparent about it.
items.markingKey: Context (Davis combined court records with informed speculation to reconstruct the lives of peasants in a famous case of identity fraud.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It shows how historians must use imagination carefully when evidence is incomplete, and be transparent about it. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the challenges historians face with limited evidence.

An historian is researching organising an argument and reflecting on the methods of historians. Explain the value and limitations of Source A for this research, with reference to its origin, purpose and content.
items.answer: Value: A considered defence of historical method by a leading historian. Limitations: It was written as a polemic against postmodernist theorists, so it may simplify their views.
items.markingKey: Value: A considered defence of historical method by a leading historian. Limitations: It was written as a polemic against postmodernist theorists, so it may simplify their views. items.stem: Explain why the investigation should be organised around an argument rather than chronology.
items.answer: An argument-based structure keeps the focus on the research question and builds a judgement, whereas chronology tends to produce narrative.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: An argument-based structure keeps the focus on the research question and builds a judgement, whereas chronology tends to produce narrative. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "A good investigation avoids discussing gaps in the evidence." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Acknowledging gaps and uncertainty shows critical understanding and strengthens the judgement.
items.markingKey: Acknowledging gaps and uncertainty shows critical understanding and strengthens the judgement. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "plagiarism"?
options: Whether a source is genuinely what it claims to be
Breaking down evidence and arguments to show how they support or challenge a judgement
Presenting the words, ideas or work of another person as one’s own without acknowledgement
The extent to which a source’s information can be trusted for a given purpose
items.answer: Presenting the words, ideas or work of another person as one’s own without acknowledgement
items.markingKey: C. "plagiarism" is presenting the words, ideas or work of another person as one’s own without acknowledgement.

items.stem: "Using AI tools to write the investigation is acceptable as long as you check the facts." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Work generated by others, including AI tools, must not be presented as one’s own; any permitted use must be acknowledged according to IB academic integrity policy.
items.markingKey: Work generated by others, including AI tools, must not be presented as one’s own; any permitted use must be acknowledged according to IB academic integrity policy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A: Mr Justice Charles Gray, judgment in Irving v. Penguin Books and Deborah Lipstadt, High Court, London, 11 April 2000 (adapted)

Irving has for his own ideological reasons persistently and deliberately misrepresented and manipulated historical evidence; he is an active Holocaust denier.

An historian is researching academic honesty and the use of sources in historical writing. Explain the value and limitations of Source A for this research, with reference to its origin, purpose and content.
items.answer: Value: A legal judgment based on detailed expert analysis (including by Richard Evans) of Irving’s use of sources. Limitations: It is a legal judgment on a libel claim, not a historical study, and addresses only the specific issues in the case.
items.markingKey: Value: A legal judgment based on detailed expert analysis (including by Richard Evans) of Irving’s use of sources. Limitations: It is a legal judgment on a libel claim, not a historical study, and addresses only the specific issues in the case. Award up to [3]: the response must refer to origin, purpose and content and link each to value or limitation for the stated enquiry; at least one value and one limitation are needed for full marks; a list of features without explaining their effect on value is capped at half marks.

items.stem: Tomás writes: "Paraphrasing a source in your own words means you do not need to cite it." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The ideas still belong to the original author and must be cited.
items.markingKey: The ideas still belong to the original author and must be cited. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from a university history department’s academic integrity guidance for students (illustrative)

Students must understand that copying wording, even with a footnote, without quotation marks is plagiarism. Every idea taken from another writer must be acknowledged.

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for an historian studying academic honesty and the use of sources in historical writing.
items.answer: Value: It shows the standards expected in academic historical writing. Limitations: It is general guidance, not specific to IB requirements, and does not discuss particular cases.
items.markingKey: Value: It shows the standards expected in academic historical writing. Limitations: It is general guidance, not specific to IB requirements, and does not discuss particular cases. Award up to [3]: the response must refer to origin, purpose and content and link each to value or limitation for the stated enquiry; at least one value and one limitation are needed for full marks; a list of features without explaining their effect on value is capped at half marks.

items.stem: Explain why the Irving v. Lipstadt case is significant for historians.
items.answer: It showed in court that deliberate manipulation of sources could be exposed by checking references, defending the integrity of historical method.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It showed in court that deliberate manipulation of sources could be exposed by checking references, defending the integrity of historical method. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the argument that academic honesty is as important as historical knowledge in the work of historians.
items.answer: Honesty is a precondition of valid history; without it, knowledge cannot be trusted.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: credibility depends on honest use of evidence; Irving case; Ambrose plagiarism; knowledge and interpretation are the substance of history; honesty is a minimum requirement rather than a skill. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Honesty is a precondition of valid history; without it, knowledge cannot be trusted. The IB internal assessment in which a student investigates a historical question of their choice using sources
The historian’s choice of which evidence to use, which shapes the argument
A focused, open question that the historical investigation sets out to answer

items.markingKey: D. "research question" is a focused, open question that the historical investigation sets out to answer.

items.stem: Distinguish between reliability and authenticity.
items.answer: Authenticity concerns whether a source is genuine; reliability concerns whether a genuine source’s content can be trusted for a purpose. A genuine source can still be unreliable.
items.markingKey: Authenticity concerns whether a source is genuine; reliability concerns whether a genuine source’s content can be trusted for a purpose. A genuine source can still be unreliable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that a good research question should cover as long a period as possible. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A focused period and topic allow depth; very broad questions lead to narrative and superficial treatment.
items.markingKey: A focused period and topic allow depth; very broad questions lead to narrative and superficial treatment. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why reflection is an important part of the historical investigation.
items.answer: It shows understanding of how historians work – selecting evidence, dealing with bias and gaps, making interpretations – and links the student’s experience to historical method.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows understanding of how historians work – selecting evidence, dealing with bias and gaps, making interpretations – and links the student’s experience to historical method. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to the plagiarism controversy surrounding Stephen Ambrose in 2002, explain how it illustrates the importance of academic honesty.
items.answer: The popular US historian was found to have copied passages from other authors in “The Wild Blue” and other books, with only footnote acknowledgement and no quotation marks. It shows that copying wording without quotation marks is plagiarism even when a source is mentioned.
items.markingKey: Context (The popular US historian was found to have copied passages from other authors in “The Wild Blue” and other books, with only footnote acknowledgement and no quotation marks.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Evidence gathered through recorded interviews with people who experienced past events"?
options: oral history
citation
reflection
authenticity
items.answer: oral history
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of oral history.

items.stem: Which of the following is the main purpose of the reflection section of the historical investigation?
options: To list every source consulted
To describe the background of the topic
To consider what the process revealed about the methods and challenges of historians
To summarise the conclusion of the investigation
items.answer: To consider what the process revealed about the methods and challenges of historians
items.markingKey: C. Reflection focuses on historical method, linked to the student’s own investigation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the reflection section and the investigation section.
items.answer: The investigation presents an argument answering the research question using evidence; the reflection considers what the process revealed about the methods and challenges of historians.
items.markingKey: The investigation presents an argument answering the research question using evidence; the reflection considers what the process revealed about the methods and challenges of historians. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Using AI tools to write the investigation is acceptable as long as you check the facts." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Work generated by others, including AI tools, must not be presented as one’s own; any permitted use must be acknowledged according to IB academic integrity policy.
items.markingKey: Work generated by others, including AI tools, must not be presented as one’s own; any permitted use must be acknowledged according to IB academic integrity policy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between authenticity and reliability.
items.answer: Authenticity concerns whether a source is genuine; reliability concerns whether a genuine source’s content can be trusted for a purpose. A genuine source can still be unreliable.
items.markingKey: Authenticity concerns whether a source is genuine; reliability concerns whether a genuine source’s content can be trusted for a purpose. A genuine source can still be unreliable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a closed research question and an open research question.
items.answer: An open question, such as “How significant…?”, requires analysis and judgement; a closed question, such as “When did…?”, has a simple factual answer.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from a university history department’s academic integrity guidance for students (illustrative)

Students must understand that copying wording, even with a footnote, without quotation marks is plagiarism. Every idea taken from another writer must be acknowledged.

Summarise the argument conveyed by Source A in relation to academic honesty and the use of sources in historical writing.
items.answer: All borrowed wording must be quoted and all borrowed ideas acknowledged, otherwise it is plagiarism.

Source A: Paraphrased from the report of the West German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv) on the “Hitler Diaries”, 6 May 1983

Tests showed that the paper contained a whitening agent not used in paper until the 1950s, and the bindings contained polyester threads. The diaries are a crude forgery.

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for an historian studying identifying and evaluating sources for a historical investigation.
items.answer: Value: An official scientific examination by the national archives, giving conclusive evidence about authenticity. Limitations: It addresses only authenticity and does not explain how the forgery was produced or why experts were deceived.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "Any interesting topic is suitable for the historical investigation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The topic must be historical, researchable with available sources and answerable within the word limit.

items.stem:
Source C: Paraphrased from Richard J. Evans, British historian, In Defence of History, 1997

History can be true, if not absolutely so. The past did happen, and historians can, with care and honesty, reach reliable, if provisional, conclusions about it.

Identify the main points that Source C makes about organising an argument and reflecting on the methods of historians, using details from the source.
items.answer: Historians can reach reliable, though not absolute, truths about the past if they work carefully.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Primary sources are always more useful than secondary sources in a historical investigation."
items.answer: Both are essential; their usefulness depends on the research question and evaluation.
